nodes.span: I will do this in three stages and try to bring it together at the end.
nodes.statement: The argument is presented as a three-stage construction of a single program.
nodes.status_reason: stated plan of exposition, not derived from anything the reader holds

nodes.span: the problem is to write a source program that, when compiled and executed, will produce as output an exact copy of its source
nodes.statement: Stage I defines the exercise of writing a self-reproducing program: one whose output is an exact copy of its own source.
nodes.status_reason: a definition the reader can check, using held terms program and compiler

nodes.span: Figure 1 shows a self-reproducing program in the C programming language
nodes.statement: Figure 1 exhibits an actual self-reproducing C program, showing the exercise is solvable.
nodes.status_reason: exhibited artifact; reader cannot derive its inner working, only accept the exhibit

nodes.span: (I) This program can be easily written by another program.
nodes.statement: Such a self-reproducing program can easily be written by another program.
nodes.status_reason: asserted of the figure with no account the reader can follow, since the figure's mechanism is symbolic and not held

nodes.span: This pro- gram can contain an arbitrary amount of excess baggage that will be reproduced along with the main algorithm
nodes.statement: Such a program can carry arbitrary extra content that is reproduced along with the reproducing algorithm.
nodes.status_reason: supported only by the observation that the comment is reproduced in the example

nodes.span: In the example, even the comment is reproduced.
nodes.statement: In Figure 1 even the comment is reproduced, illustrating the excess-baggage property.
nodes.status_reason: direct observation of the exhibited example

nodes.span: The C compiler is written in C.
nodes.statement: The C compiler is itself written in C, creating chicken-and-egg problems.
nodes.status_reason: stated fact of the setting, available to a reader holding the term compiler

nodes.span: C allows a string construct to specify an initialized character array
nodes.statement: C strings allow escaped characters to represent unprintable characters such as newline.
nodes.status_reason: stated language fact with an illustration

nodes.span: The act of knowing then allows it to recompile itself, thus perpetuating the knowledge.
nodes.statement: The compiler's escape-handling code knows the newline code portably and perpetuates that knowledge by recompiling itself.
nodes.status_reason: follows from the compiler being written in C (n7) plus the escape construct (n8)

nodes.span: Suppose we wish to alter the C compiler to include the sequence "\v" to represent the vertical tab character.
nodes.statement: Stage II attempts to extend the compiler to recognize a new escape sequence in the portable self-referencing style.
nodes.status_reason: a step taken on the code described in n9

nodes.span: since the binary version of the compiler does not know about "\v," the source is not legal C
nodes.statement: The extension cannot be compiled directly because the existing binary does not yet recognize the new sequence.
nodes.status_reason: follows from n10 with the self-referential structure of n9

nodes.span: We look up on an ASCII chart that a vertical tab is decimal 11. We alter our source to look like Figure 4.
nodes.statement: The compiler is 'trained' by temporarily hard-coding the numeric character value so the old compiler accepts the new source.
nodes.status_reason: a remedy stated in response to the failure in n11

nodes.span: We install the resulting binary as the new official C compiler and now we can write the portable version
nodes.statement: Once the trained binary is installed as official, the source can revert to the portable self-referencing form and knowledge persists in the binary.
nodes.status_reason: follows from n12 and the self-perpetuation in n9

nodes.span: It is as close to a "learning" program as I have seen. You simply tell it once
nodes.statement: The compiler thereby behaves like a learning program: told once, it retains a self-referencing definition.
nodes.status_reason: a characterization of the process in n13

nodes.span: Figure 6 shows a simple modification to the compiler that will deliberately miscompile source whenever a particular pattern is matched
nodes.statement: Stage III modifies the compiler's control loop to deliberately miscompile source whenever a chosen pattern is matched.
nodes.status_reason: a construction shown in a figure, checkable but not derived from held results

nodes.span: Since it is deliberate, it should be called a "Trojan horse."
nodes.statement: Such a deliberate miscompilation is properly called a Trojan horse rather than a bug.
nodes.status_reason: terminological consequence of n15's deliberateness

nodes.span: The actual bug I planted in the compiler would match code in the UNIX "login" command
nodes.statement: The author actually planted such a pattern matching the UNIX login command, letting the replacement code accept a known password.
nodes.status_reason: first-hand report offered as instance of n15

nodes.span: if this code were installed in binary and the binary were used to compile the login command, I could log into that system as any user
nodes.statement: A binary compiler containing this Trojan grants the attacker login as any user on systems whose login was compiled with it.
nodes.status_reason: follows from n15/n17 given the ordinary meaning of compiling and installing

nodes.span: Such blatant code would not go undetected for long. Even the most casual perusal of the source
nodes.statement: Leaving the Trojan visible in the compiler source would soon be detected, so a hiding step is needed.
nodes.status_reason: plausible assertion about inspection, not derived

nodes.span: The second pattern is aimed at the C compiler. The replacement code is a Stage I self-reproducing program that inserts both Trojan horses
nodes.statement: A second Trojan is added whose pattern targets the compiler itself and whose replacement is a self-reproducing program inserting both Trojans.
nodes.status_reason: built from the Stage I reproducing program (n3,n4,n5) and the Stage III modification (n15)

nodes.span: First we compile the modified source with the normal C compiler to produce a bugged binary. We install this binary as the official C.
nodes.statement: The doubly bugged source is compiled once with a clean compiler and the resulting binary installed as the official compiler.
nodes.status_reason: the training step of Stage II (n12,n13) applied to n20

nodes.span: We can now remove the bugs from the source of the compiler and the new binary will reinsert the bugs whenever it is compiled
nodes.statement: After installation the bugs can be deleted from the source, yet the binary reinserts them at every recompilation.
nodes.status_reason: follows from n20 and n21 via the self-perpetuation mechanism of n14

nodes.span: the login command will remain bugged with no trace in source anywhere
nodes.statement: The login backdoor persists with no trace in any source code.
nodes.status_reason: combines n18 with the source-erasure result n22

nodes.span: You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself.
nodes.statement: You cannot trust code you did not create entirely yourself.
nodes.status_reason: drawn as the moral of the constructed attack n23

nodes.span: No amount of source-level verification or scrutiny will protect you from using untrusted code.
nodes.statement: Source-level verification and scrutiny cannot protect against such an attack.
nodes.status_reason: follows directly from the no-trace-in-source result n23

nodes.span: I could have picked on any program-handling program such as an assembler, a loader, or even hardware microcode
nodes.statement: The attack generalizes to any program-handling program, including assemblers, loaders and microcode.
nodes.status_reason: asserted by analogy without a derivation for the other cases

nodes.span: As the level of program gets lower, these bugs will be harder and harder to detect.
nodes.statement: The lower the level of the compromised program, the harder the bug is to detect, with microcode nearly undetectable.
nodes.status_reason: plausible extrapolation from n26, no argument given

nodes.span: The acts performed by these kids are vandalism at best and probably trespass and theft at worst.
nodes.statement: Press coverage of hackers is wrong because their acts amount to vandalism, trespass and theft.
nodes.status_reason: moral judgement asserted, independent of the technical argument

nodes.span: Unauthorized access to computer systems is already a serious crime in a few states
nodes.statement: Unauthorized access is already a serious crime in some states and is being legislated in more.
nodes.status_reason: reported legal fact offered in support of the moral claim

nodes.span: There is an explosive situation brewing.
nodes.statement: A dangerous gap exists between glorification of intruders by media and impending severe punishment.
nodes.status_reason: drawn from n28 and the legislative trend n29

nodes.span: I have watched kids testifying before Congress. It is clear that they are completely unaware
nodes.statement: Observation of youths testifying before Congress shows they are unaware of the seriousness of their acts.
nodes.status_reason: first-hand observation offered in support

nodes.span: The act of breaking into a computer system has to have the same social stigma as breaking into a neighbor's house.
nodes.statement: Breaking into a computer system should carry the same social stigma as burglary, regardless of weak security.
nodes.status_reason: prescription drawn from the cultural gap n30 and n31

nodes.span: I first read of the possibility of such a Trojan horse in an Air Force critique (4)
nodes.statement: The possibility of such a Trojan horse was first read of in an Air Force critique of an early Multics implementation.
nodes.status_reason: citation of prior source, unverifiable reference
